title: The Irregular Verbs
short: A few common verbs are irregular: rdj/dj "give", jj/jw "come", jnj "bring", wnn "be, exist".
trouble: Students fail to recognize dj as rdj. The r often drops in writing; both are the verb "give".

blocks.html: Most verbs follow the class rules of Verb Classes. A few very common verbs do not. Gardiner calls them anomalous; you will meet them on every page, so they are worth learning now.

The irregular verbs to know: rdj "give" (often written dj), jj or jw "come", and, with quirks of their own, jnj "bring" (stem jn) and wnn "be, exist" (stem wn). Their commands are special words: jmj "give!" and mj "come!".

These are the verbs people used most, and the most-used words in any language keep old irregular forms (think of English "be, am, was" or "go, went"). Egyptian rdj lost its r in speech in many forms, so the scribes often wrote only dj. The verb "come" had two stems, jj and jw, and different forms chose different ones.

blocks.cap: You have read rdj without its r already: the conical loaf dj in ḥtp-dj-nsw.

blocks.title: Find the verb
blocks.q: Under which verb do you look up jn.n=f "he brought"?
steps: Take off .n=f: the stem is jn.
No common verb is just jn; add the weak j: jnj "bring".

blocks.title: Where did the r go?
blocks.q: Is dj=f the same verb as rdj.n=f?
steps: dj is rdj without its r, a very common writing.
dj=f "he gives" and rdj.n=f "he gave" are both forms of rdj "give".

blocks.title: A command
steps: jmj is the special command form used for rdj "give": "give!".

blocks.html: Not recognizing dj as rdj. Because the r so often drops in writing, students look up dj and find nothing, or think it is a different verb. Check: whenever you see the conical loaf (X8) or the arm holding a loaf (D37) in a verb, think of rdj "give".
wnn "be, exist" also serves as a helping verb that lets other constructions stand where a verb form is needed. You will meet it again with the pseudoverbal construction.
